The real question is whether the time needed to mature the software is short enough to matter before better-funded alternatives lock in. Maybe @jiahanjimliu can add some color here. As I am not a software engineer.

Well Putting it together: the narrative of multi-host, rack-scale, switch-based CXL pooling capturing a $15 to $16 billion market in the 2026-2028 window is, in my view, low probability.  The leading switch player Marvell, via its XConn acquisition, guides that business to only about $100 million by fiscal 2028, and that figure even includes PCIe, not just CXL. That's one company's early-ramp revenue two years out

So where are the best risk-adjusted returns? In my opinion, still the bits makers SK Hynix and Micron, with SK leading and Micron second. Samsung I'd put a tier below for now since it's slipped its own CXL timelines more than once. Hope they learned. Current execution seems they have but let’s see.

The reason I land on the producers is simple: they win whether the demand shows up as expansion OR pooling, on AMD OR Arm, in CPU racks OR GPU racks.

But "wins either way" is only half true. Because it’s still a bet on the DRAM shortage. CXL expansion demand is shortage-conditional, and so are the bits makers' earnings. If DRAM normalizes arbitrage decays It's still one concentrated bet that the shortage persists, dressed as optionality. I think it persists into 2028+ so I'm comfortable. But know that's the bet.

And that brings me back to my punchline. This is essentially the memory-supercycle trade with CXL as a free option on top. It is NOT a clever CXL-specific edge and the most valuable thing I got out of analyzing CXL this hard is realizing it doesn't change the trade I'd already want to make. Keep my primary exposure in SK Hynix and Micron, and treat CXL as upside on top of the DRAM and HBM cycle.

If you want a pure-play like Astera, understand what you're paying for: a huge premium for flawless execution, against a CXL market that's small near-term and whose best use case the warm KV-cache tier NVIDIA is actively contesting from inside its own software stack.

Even then, I'd probably still keep playing the theme through the big memory suppliers: SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung mostly and then a potential name that isnt priced for perfection. 

That’s my read. If you’re closer to the pooling-software/hardware stack than I am, I’m listening otherwise this is where I land.

post.text:
$MU Q3 2026 earnings: A Blowout Quarter, Bought at the Top of the Cycle

*** Updated after the call:

Micron delivered a record-shattering quarter: revenue hit $41.5B, up 346% YoY and 74% sequentially—the largest dollar increase in company history. Non-GAAP gross margin reached 84.9% and EPS was $25.11. Q4 guidance calls for $50B revenue and $31 EPS, both records. The headline news is structural: 16 new Strategic Customer Agreements lock in roughly $100B of minimum-price revenue and bring $22B in customer financial commitments. The catch—management itself flagged that price increases are now moderating, and a $31B receivables balance is the first sign that converting this boom to cash is getting harder.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲
𝗗𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗟𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗜𝗻: 16 multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements cover ~20% of DRAM and ~30% of NAND volume, with $100B in minimum-price revenue and $22B of customer commitments ($18B cash deposits). Management says even floor prices deliver margins well above any prior peak.
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲: Management now expects DRAM and NAND to stay tight beyond calendar 2027—pushed out from the prior 'beyond 2026' view. New fab capacity takes years, while AI demand keeps climbing, supporting pricing far longer than a normal cycle.

🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲
𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴: The 86% Q4 gross margin guide reflects what management called a 'meaningful moderation in the rate of price increases.' At this altitude, incremental price yields little additional margin. Memory pricing is at or near a cyclical peak.
𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗺: Receivables ballooned to $31.0B from $9.3B at fiscal year-end—a $20B nine-month drag that held operating cash flow ($45.7B) just below net income ($47.3B). Rapid revenue growth is outrunning collections.

⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁
🟢 Bullish, with one eye on the exit. Results are exceptional and the SCAs add genuine durability. But the buyer is paying peak-cycle margins right as management signals price growth is slowing, and a $31B receivables build is the first crack in the cash story. Outstanding quarter; not a max-bullish entry point.

— • — • —

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀

New: 🟢🟢 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
Micron signed 16 SCAs spanning data center, consumer, and auto—four very large customers, three mid-sized, the rest automotive. These take-or-pay contracts run five years (2026-2030; auto is three). 14 of the 16 carry ~$100B in cumulative minimum-price revenue, and customers are putting up $22B in commitments, ~$18B as cash deposits. The largest deals set ceiling prices at current CQ2 levels and floors that still clear prior-peak margins. When fully executed, ~40% of revenue sits under fixed or ceiling pricing.

🟢🟢 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮 $𝟭𝟬𝟬𝗕 𝗥𝘂𝗻 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗲
Data center revenue topped $25B in the quarter—an annualized run rate above $100B. The Core Data Center unit grew 103% sequentially as agentic AI extends demand beyond accelerators into CPU and storage racks. Data center SLC revenue alone exceeded $5B, more than doubling sequentially. Management raised its calendar 2026 server-unit outlook to high-teens growth, up from low-double-digits.

🟢🟢 𝗗𝗥𝗔𝗠 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗡𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗕𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝗥𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲
DRAM revenue hit a record $31.3B (76% of total, +67% sequentially) on low-single-digit bit growth and a low-60s percent price jump. NAND hit a record $9.9B (24% of total, +99% sequentially) on mid-single-digit bit growth and a mid-80s percent price increase. Almost all of the growth is price, not volume—the defining feature of this cycle and the reason margins exploded.

New: 🔴 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗦𝗽𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Receivables jumped to $31.0B from $17.3B last quarter and $9.3B at fiscal year-end—roughly tripling in nine months. The $20B build was the single largest working-capital drag in the cash flow statement and is why nine-month operating cash flow ($45.7B) came in just below net income ($47.3B). With revenue set to climb further to $50B, monitoring whether collections keep pace is essential; this is the one data point that cuts against an otherwise pristine quarter.

New: ⚪ 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴
The Q4 gross margin guide of ~86% is up only ~1 point from 84.9%, versus the 10-point sequential jumps seen earlier in the year. Management explicitly attributed this to a 'meaningful moderation in the rate of price increases.' At these levels, incremental pricing barely moves the margin line. This is the clearest signal that the steepest part of the pricing ramp is behind the company, even if absolute levels stay elevated.

🔴 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗘𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆
Management expects PC and smartphone unit volumes to decline even as industry revenue grows, because high memory prices are pricing out some buyers. Micron is steering scarce bits toward data center and high-value applications, but the admission that consumer units fall under these prices is a reminder that the pricing that drives today's margins also destroys some end demand.

⚪ 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗘𝘅 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗚𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸
FY26 capital spending is now ~$27B, with Q4 alone near $10B, and FY27 stepping up further—over half the year-over-year increase is construction. Idaho ID1 targets first wafers mid-calendar 2027, ID2 in late 2028, with New York, Japan, Singapore, and Taiwan all in flight. Delivering these greenfield projects on schedule is the gating factor for future supply; any slip pushes out the volume needed to sustain growth once price gains fade.

🟢 𝗛𝗕𝗠𝟰 𝗥𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗲
HBM4 12-high is ramping twice as fast as HBM3E 12-high, with over $1B already shipped and mature yields expected sooner than the prior generation. Micron is deliberately holding HBM share close to its overall DRAM share—because HBM's high wafer trade ratio (over 3x and rising toward 4x for HBM4E) consumes capacity that would otherwise serve non-HBM markets. Notably, management confirmed non-HBM margins currently exceed HBM margins, a mix nuance worth watching as HBM grows.

🟢 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘁𝘀 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿
Micron cut total debt to $5.7B from $14.6B at fiscal year-end, ending with a $24.4B net cash position and $30.2B in cash and investments. All three rating agencies upgraded the company this year, reaching BBB+. From December 2026, after the second anniversary of its CHIPS agreement, management intends to return 100% of excess cash to shareholders over time—a meaningful shift now that buyback restrictions ease.

— • — • —

𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀

𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻, 𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗚𝗔𝗔𝗣 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): 𝟴𝟭.𝟮%
Accelerating, then plateauing. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded from 26.8% a year ago to 69.0% last quarter to 81.2% this quarter—a 54-point YoY swing. Every business unit posted operating margins above 60%, led by Mobile & Client at 86% (versus 15% a year ago, when that unit ran near breakeven). The operating leverage is extraordinary, but with the Q4 gross margin guide flagged as moderating, this quarter likely marks the steepest part of the climb.

𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄, 𝗔𝗱𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭𝟴.𝟯 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻
A quarterly record, up from $6.9B last quarter and $1.9B a year ago. Built from $25.4B operating cash flow less $7.1B net CapEx. Crucially, this excludes SCA customer deposits, which management says flow through financing—not free cash flow—and will be returned to customers in the back half of the agreement terms. Cash and investments reached a record $30.2B.

𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗢𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (𝗥𝗣𝗢): 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿 $𝟱 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗱), ~$𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲)
Under ASC 606, Micron began disclosing RPO this quarter. The reported figure exceeds $5B—only the SCAs closed within Q3, with ~$1.8B of associated next-12-month revenue (mostly smaller auto deals). Once all 14-of-16 priced agreements are reflected in the Q4 10-K, RPO jumps to ~$100B. Management stressed this is a conservative minimum—based on floor volumes and floor prices—and expects actual revenue to exceed it substantially.

— • — • —

𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗙𝗤𝟰-𝟮𝟲 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲: $𝟱𝟬.𝟬 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 ± $𝟭.𝟬 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻
Decelerating in rate, still a record. The $50B midpoint implies ~21% sequential growth, down from this quarter's 74% pace—a natural slowing off a vastly larger base. It would mark a sixth consecutive quarterly revenue record.

𝗙𝗤𝟰-𝟮𝟲 𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗚𝗔𝗔𝗣 𝗘𝗣𝗦: $𝟯𝟭.𝟬𝟬 ± $𝟭.𝟬𝟬
The midpoint implies ~23% sequential growth from $25.11, slightly outpacing revenue growth as margins tick up. Based on ~1.15B diluted shares.

𝗙𝗤𝟰-𝟮𝟲 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻: 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝟴𝟲% (𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗚𝗔𝗔𝗣)
Decelerating expansion. Up roughly 1 point from 84.9%, versus the 10-point jumps of recent quarters. Management directly attributed the smaller step to a moderation in the rate of price increases—the key tell that pricing momentum is cooling even as levels stay high.

𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟳 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀 & 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗘𝘅: 𝗢𝗽𝗘𝘅 +$𝟭𝗕; 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗘𝘅 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗤𝟰 𝗿𝘂𝗻-𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲
Operating expenses will rise about $1B in fiscal 2027 to fund R&D, weighted to the second half. FY26 CapEx lands near $27B (Q4 ~$10B), and FY27 quarterly CapEx runs above Q4 levels, with more than half the year-over-year increase coming from construction as Micron pulls in clean-room capacity. Spending is rising into a period of slowing price gains—a setup that pressures near-term free cash flow conversion.

— • — • —

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻

post.text:
《为什么上周五美股内存老师们集体开始提示波动大、减仓和伟大撤退了》

宏观今年年底有加息预期、美光财报、海力士赴美上市、苹果涨价并游说采购长鑫存储

宏观前提：6月17日美联储把利率维持在 3.50%–3.75%(从去年12月就没动过)，投票12比0全票通过。但底下的点阵图转向鹰派：多数官员现在预计2026年底利率会比现在更高，中值升到3.8%，等于暗示今年还要再加一次息；18位官员里有17位认为通胀风险偏上行。

1️⃣上周时间线

6/24 — 供给端炸裂（利好）

-美光发创纪录财报：营收约 414.6 亿美元、同比 +346%，毛利率 84.6%，下季度指引 86%。股价当天约 +16%。
-同日，SK海力士宣布赴美上市（见下）。

6/25 — 需求端裂缝（转折点）

-苹果跌 6.12% 到 275.15 美元，自 2025 年 4 月股灾以来最差一天。
-原因：苹果宣布 Mac 涨价 15–20%、iPad 涨 15–25%（每台贵 100–300 美元），理由是内存太贵扛不住；iPhone 暂不涨（怕需求被price跑）。库克称这是内存成本的"百年一遇的洪水"。
-关键含义：连全世界议价能力最强的买家都被逼到转嫁成本 → 短缺是真的（利好），但同时暴露了"高价会毁掉终端需求"这个天花板（利空预期）。

6/27–6/28 — 供给的新苗头

-传出苹果为降成本，想从被列入黑名单的中国厂商长鑫存储(CXMT)采购。花旗把长鑫描述为可信的全球第四大 DRAM 厂。
-注意区分：长鑫只产普通 DRAM、不产 HBM，对美光的 HBM 高利润业务威胁有限。但标题本身动摇了"永久短缺"的故事。

7/10（计划）— SK海力士赴美上市

-在纳斯达克发 ADR（代码 SKHY），融资约 294 亿美元，发1779万股新股。
-钱用来建龙仁新厂、清州封装厂、买 EUV 光刻机——即"扩产"。
-背景：海力士股价一年涨约 850%、市值破万亿美元、一度超三星成韩国第一。韩股估值低（约8倍前瞻PE），赴美意在缩小与美光的估值差。
-盘面：消息出来周四曾涨超12%，周五又在全球科技股抛售里跌8%——市场两极、脚下不稳。

2️⃣这些事件蕴含了什么问题

（1）总开关：美联储转鹰，杀估值

6/17 美联储维持 3.50–3.75%，但点阵图翻鹰：2026年底中值升到3.8%（暗示要加息），17/18 认为通胀风险偏上行。年初市场还预期降息1–2次。

为什么翻：通胀因伊朗战争的油价冲击又黏住（核心PCE 3.0%→3.3%，WTI 一度冲到113美元）；就业强；新主席沃什鹰派。

对你这条线的意义：内存/AI 是估值最贵的成长股，它们的高估值部分建立在"未来会降息"上。这个预期被抽掉甚至反向 = 直接杀估值。

张力（值得写）：AI 既是繁荣引擎，也是利率降不下来的部分原因（巨额capex是刺激性投资需求）；但沃什又认为AI长期反通胀。两头拽。

（2）供给：美光报喜 + 海力士融资 = 周期顶部的双重信号

两个主角，同一周，讲的是供给端的两面：

👉美光（卖家的"现在有多爽"）

创纪录财报：营收约414.6亿美元、同比+346%，毛利率 84.6%，下季度指引 86%，股价当天约+16%。

利好里藏的警报：这种"利润爆表、毛利率历史新高"恰恰是周期股最危险的位置。高固定成本行业里，价格一反转毛利率会比营收先崩——所以别被84%毛利率冲昏头，它越漂亮，离顶可能越近。判断拐点要盯毛利率，不是营收。

👉海力士（卖家的"拿钱去干嘛"）

赴美上市融294亿，钱明确用于建龙仁新厂、清州封装、买EUV——即扩产。

空头逻辑闭环：高价的解药就是高价。利润创纪录 → 厂商趁股价高融钱 → 建更多产能 → 2027–2028供给上来 → 周期反转。海力士这294亿就是这条链的实锤（建厂要几年，是远期变量）。

加一个观察：公司往往在估值最贵、市场最热时发新股圈钱——这是周期偏后段的常见动作。

两个合起来的味道：一个在报"现在赚翻了"，一个在拿这份热度融钱扩产。"赚最多的时候"和"扩产最猛的时候"撞在一起，正是周期股见顶的经典画面。

（3）需求：苹果暴露了天花板

逻辑：内存贵 → 电子产品涨价15–25% → 人们少买 → 内存需求最终下来。

这是市场关注点从"谁有货"转向"谁有真需求"的第一个实锤。

post.text:
今天美股收盘，表面看挺平静，标普基本没动，里头其实藏着一出好戏。

主角还是美光。它单日成交逼近 1000 亿美元，股价再创历史新高，存储这条线现在谁都挡不住。按理说龙头这么猛，大盘该跟着乐，可纳指偏偏收跌了 0.46%。

问题出在苹果和微软身上。这两家同一天宣布给 iPhone 和 Xbox 涨价，理由说得很直接——内存太贵，扛不住了。市场一听就反应过来：美光赚的钱，有一部分是从苹果微软的成本里抠出来的。结果苹果当天跌 6%，微软跌 3%，两个权重巨头一塌，直接把纳指拖下了水。

这是内存超级周期走到现在最值得琢磨的一面。前半段大家只看到涨价等于芯片厂赚翻，美光、海力士、三星吃得满嘴流油；现在后半段来了，买内存的那些硬件厂开始喊疼，要么自己利润被压，要么把成本转给消费者。同一个涨价，芯片厂是受益的一方，设备厂是买单的一方，今天市场第一次把这笔账算得这么清楚。

再说美光那个 1000 亿成交。这个数字风光，但老股民看到会先皱眉。历史上特斯拉、英伟达都出现过单日千亿成交，事后回看，往往是情绪到顶附近的信号之一。倒不是说立刻就要见顶，而是该进场的钱差不多都进齐了，再往上得靠新的故事接力。

圈里现在吵成两派。一派盯着美光那个个位数的 forward PE，喊这么便宜不冲等什么；另一派说成交都炸成这样了，该让它歇口气。两边都有道理，区别只在你是做趋势的还是做波段的。还有个容易被忽略的点，这次美光财报真正的隐藏赢家其实是闪迪 SNDK，跟着存储一起水涨船高，只盯美光一只的人可能错过了这块。

宏观这边也没闲着。5 月的 PCE 出来了，年率 4.1%，破了 4，是 2023 年 4 月以来最高。美联储的通胀目标是 2%，现在等于翻了一倍。月率比预期低了 0.1 个点，算个小安慰，但 4% 这个数摆在台面上，美联储很快降息的故事就讲不顺了。利率敏感的科技成长股对这个最敏感，今天纳指走弱，这份数据是有份的。

最后提一句联动。海力士绑着韩国股指，韩股又绑着美股芯片，这几天韩股动不动就熔断，等于给美股芯片埋了根引线。手里有存储仓位的，除了盯美光财报，也得分点注意力给韩股那边的波动。

一天下来，结论不复杂：美光基本面没问题，问题是它太热了，热到开始反噬自己的产业链，热到成交量发出见顶警告。拿着的人不用慌，但这个位置追高要小心，给自己留点回调接货的空间。谈不上看空，就是提醒一句，别在情绪最高的时候替自己做决定。#mu #海力士 #dram

$MU $DRAM Micron’s SCA doesn’t just lock in revenue. They restructure the market, splitting it into a contracted layer and a spot layer, then using contracted lockups to mechanically inflate spot pricing. Micron’s 20% DRAM coverage isn’t “too little.” It’s precisely enough to satisfy Wall Street while preserving maximum spot upside.

Here’s why.

Micron signed 16 strategic customer agreements in FQ3, covering ~20% of DRAM shipments and a third of NAND. The market focused on the $100B minimum revenue commitment and $22B in deposits. But the most informative number isn’t $100B. It’s that 20%.

If management believed DRAM pricing was near its peak, the rational move would be to lock in as much volume as possible at current prices. Sign 50%, sign 60%, crystallize peak pricing into contracts. Instead they signed 20%. 80% of DRAM shipments are still priced on quarterly spot or short-term contracts. That ratio is management’s revealed judgment on where pricing is headed: they don’t think we’re at the top.

This also explains why the agreement price ceilings are anchored at current CQ2 market prices. If management thought this was the peak, capping at current levels would offer zero benefit to the seller. A ceiling only matters if you expect spot to exceed it. Management set the ceiling, then left 80% of volume outside it. Translation: they expect spot to rise above the ceiling, and that 80% will ship at those higher prices.

The CFO reinforced this on the earnings call: RPO at floor pricing is an accounting measure, and they fully expect actual revenue to come in well above it. $100B is minimum volume times minimum price. Actual will be “much higher.” The excess comes from two sources: contracted volume settling at the ceiling rather than the floor, and uncontracted volume settling at spot prices above the ceiling.

Demand hasn’t decreased. All of that demand is now competing for a shrinking pool of available supply. Spot prices get pushed up mechanically. Then the higher spot price becomes the ceiling anchor for the next round of agreements. Higher ceiling → more volume locked away → thinner spot pool → higher spot → even higher ceiling next round. A self-reinforcing loop.

The supplier doesn’t need to “raise prices.” It just needs to drain enough water from the public pool into a private reservoir. The buyers left in the shallow pool will naturally bid higher. 80% of uncovered volume transacts at those elevated prices.

Those who truly make money in investing don’t try to predict the market every day. They focus on distinguishing noise from the real variables that drive long-term trends.

Recent days brought several new variables:
- Military conflict reignited after the US-Iran ceasefire, driving risk aversion and pressuring tech stocks.

Micron $MU ’s report showed raised guidance, HBM demand far exceeds supply, orders locked in, and CapEx continuing to rise. The company and customers are both betting on sustained growth.

There won’t be a sudden stop in AI investment, only a gradual easing. Microsoft $MSFT , Meta $META , Amazon $AMZN , and Alphabet $GOOGL  have given no signals of slowing down. As long as demand exceeds supply, the AI cycle continues.

The biggest opportunities are shifting from GPUs to memory (HBM, DRAM), advanced packaging, optical modules, high-speed networking, PCBs, power supplies, liquid cooling, power grids, and data center infrastructure.

My investment philosophy stays simple. I only ask three questions:

In the short term the market fluctuates with sentiment. In the long term stock prices return to corporate value. We stay patient, respect the trend, dynamically adjust positions, avoid chasing and panicking, and wait for the next high-probability setup.

Truly excellent investors don’t trade every day — they do the right thing at the right time.

那风险到底在哪。

华尔街给美光的目标价，从 435 一直喊到 1750，这已经不是看涨多少的分歧，而是 AI 到底有没有真的改写内存周期，两拨人世界观就不一样。站在这个位置上的存储股，赌的早就不是财报好不好，财报大概率很好，赌的是指引能不能再超过市场已经打满的那套预期。一旦利好兑现、指引又没给出超预期的惊喜，就该轮到高位股消化了。

The market is already leaning defensive after his first FOMC meeting, where the message was clear: inflation is still the priority, even if it means keeping policy tight for longer. That strengthened the dollar, pushed Treasury yields higher, and made investors move away from risk assets. With Core PCE still sitting around 3.4%, I wouldn't be surprised if inflation remains a key talking point again.

Going into today's speech, I've planned for two different outcomes rather than trying to guess which one plays out.

If Warsh reinforces the idea that rates may need to stay higher for longer or even hints that another hike can't be ruled out, I'd expect the dollar and Treasury yields to climb again. That would likely keep pressure on growth stocks, so I'll be avoiding overbought tech names like Micron($MU ) and SanDisk until the market finds a stronger base. In that environment, I'd rather look for short opportunities after confirmation than fight the trend.

On the other hand, if he spends more time discussing growth risks and takes a more balanced, data-dependent approach, the market could finally get the relief it has been waiting for. A softer dollar would improve risk appetite, and I'd be watching broad market exposure through NAS100 and SPY rather than immediately chasing individual stocks.

One thing I found interesting after looking deeper into the event is that the speech isn't really about announcing the next rate move. Investors are paying closer attention to how Warsh frames inflation, the Fed's policy path, and the strength of the dollar. post.text:
Long read but worth it from an investment perspective

I want you guys to see something.

The first major public warning about a coming memory constraint came from Mehrotra during $MU Q1'24 earnings call. Shortly after, Noh-jung echoed the same message. Since then, leaders across the industry, including Tae-won, Huang and others, have been repeating it for well over a year.

I'm not saying you need to become a die-hard memory bull or bear.

I'm saying you need to understand how markets work.

High prices signal producers to expand capacity. Over time, that additional capacity helps resolve the depth of shortages. That's just basic economics. 

Now combine that with finance.

Markets are forward looking. They don't wait for the shortage to end. They begin pricing in what the supply and demand picture will look like 6, 12 or even 24 months from now. That's one reason many memory stocks moved +1,000% before the industry reached peak earnings.

There's another concept worth understanding, market efficiency.

Once information becomes widely known, the market begins incorporating it into prices. By the time everyone is talking about a memory shortage, institutional investors have likely spent months modeling when supply will catch demand and what earnings look like on the other side.

That doesn't mean the cycle is over tomorrow, in fact, none of this tells you what happens next.

It simply means that knowing today's story isn't enough. The real question is whether tomorrow will be better or worse than what the market already expects.

That's where the edge has always been. 

For scalpers, you'll be able to trade the upside in this and the downside. From an investor POV, you have to think about basically what I described above.

post.text:
The AI Buildout Is Becoming a Supply Chain Inflation Story

This chart is a map of cost pressure moving through the physical infrastructure behind AI.

The January forecast already showed tight supply across key materials. The April update is much worse. DRAM moved from roughly 150% expected 2026 price growth to 250% to 280%. NAND moved from roughly 100% to 200% to 250%. ABF substrates, CCL, and other board level materials were also revised higher.

That matters because the AI trade is no longer only about GPUs, models, or software. It is becoming a real world supply chain story.

Memory, substrates, glass, copper clad laminate, passive components, and high end board materials are now part of the bottleneck.

Why MLCCs Matter

The MLCC line is especially interesting.

MLCCs are multilayer ceramic capacitors. They are small, boring, and easy to ignore until the system cannot ship without them.

Modern AI servers and accelerator boards require enormous numbers of these parts for power delivery, filtering, and signal stability. The individual part may not be expensive, but the dependency is massive.

That is why passive components can suddenly become critical. They sit quietly in the background until demand overwhelms capacity. Then a tiny part becomes a major production constraint.

That said, the 5x to 10x claim needs to be handled carefully. The Goldman chart itself does not show a broad MLCC price increase of that magnitude. The April update shows MLCC price expectations around 0% to 5% for 2026, while the supply demand outlook shifts toward very tight.

The real point is not that MLCC prices have already exploded across the board.

The point is that the setup for a delayed repricing is forming if allocation tightens and buyers start scrambling for supply.

The Macro Read

The deeper message is that AI may be deflationary in the long run, but it is inflationary during the buildout phase.

Before AI reduces costs for the economy, it raises demand for memory, storage, servers, power equipment, cooling, land, electricity, substrates, and components.

That is what this chart is showing.

The digital story is colliding with physical scarcity.

This is also why the AI trade is splitting. The suppliers are the check receivers. The hyperscalers are the check writers.

Memory makers, substrate suppliers, advanced PCB material companies, high end passive component makers, and power infrastructure companies can benefit from tight supply.

The hyperscalers face the opposite problem. They may have real AI demand, but if the cost of building capacity keeps rising, free cash flow and margins come under pressure.

That is how AI capex can be bullish for suppliers while becoming a burden for the companies funding the buildout.

What Happens Next

My view is that bottleneck suppliers keep pricing power longer than the market expects.

The next phase of the AI trade will not just be about who has the best model. It will be about who controls scarce physical inputs.

The second risk is inventory hoarding. Once buyers believe shortages are structural, they pull orders forward, sign long term agreements, double order, and pay up for allocation. That can make shortages worse before eventually creating a correction if demand expectations cool.

The third risk is margin pressure at the hyperscaler level. If AI infrastructure costs keep rising faster than monetization, the market will start asking harder questions about return on invested capital.

This chart is saying the AI boom has entered the unglamorous phase.

Not demos.

Not headlines.

Components, substrates, lead times, allocation, and cost inflation.

That is where infrastructure booms separate the real winners from the companies simply paying the bill.

China's tungsten export restrictions, WF6 supply concerns spill over HBM and AI semiconductors.

The production risk of advanced memory and logic is increasing due to the impact of the Japanese WF6 procurement.

The increase in production of AI semiconductors is also spreading its impact on the supply network of special gases for electronics. Due to China's export restrictions on high-purity tungsten and APT, concerns about the supply of tungsten hexaffuride (WF6) supplied by Japanese manufacturers have increased, and new risks in the supply chain for the production of HBM, DRAM, advanced logic, and 3D NAND is emerging.

According to Cryptopolitan, a U.S. media outlet, the expansion of investment in AI data centers and China's tungsten export restrictions overlap, and the supply and demand of specialty gases for electronics used in semiconductor etching and film formation processes are tight. The bottleneck is not on the production capacity of the foundry and the post-process, but the material side that supports semiconductor manufacturing.

China International Finance (CICC) analyzed in a recent report that the expansion of AI infrastructure investment and China's tungsten export regulations are simultaneously putting pressure on the supply of special gases for electronics. It is said that it may affect the production of advanced processors used in data centers, AI servers, and cloud inference systems for large-scale language models (LLMs).

The mass adoption of AI is increasing not only the production of semiconductors but also the amount of gas used for each process. According to Nanda Optoelectronics, special gases for electronics account for about 13% of wafer manufacturing materials, second only to silicon wafers.

The more miniaturization progresses, the more gas demand will increase. According to the report, the 65-nanometer (nm) process requires about 20 etchings per wafer, while 7nm, which is mainly used in AI accelerators, increases to about 140 times. The more tip the tip, the more special gas consumption increases.

The increase in HBM production is also spurring the expansion of demand. Special gases such as WF6 are essential for the formation of HBM's silicon-through electrode (TSV). In addition, as the number of 3D NAND layers increases against the background of storage demand for AI, the use of related gases continues to increase.

Investment indicators show the same trend. TrendForce predicted that sales in the global foundry market in 2026 would reach $218.8 billion, an increase of 24.8% year-on-year. CICC also expects that capital investment in eight major cloud service companies will increase by about 61% and the number of AI server shipments will also increase by about 28%.

The biggest variable in terms of supply is China's tungsten export restrictions. In February last year, China introduced a licensing system for the export of major strategic minerals, including tungsten. After that, it is reported that Japanese WF6 manufacturers Kanto Denka Kogyo and Central Glass informed that their inventory for Korean customers was almost low, and it would be difficult to guarantee a stable supply until the second half of 2026. WF6 is an important material used to form tungsten wiring with advanced logic, DRAM, HBM, and 3D NAND.

The limited replacement of suppliers is also an issue. Japanese companies account for about 24% of the world's WF6 production, but it is said that it is difficult to replace it in a short period of time with a Western supply network such as the United States.

存储板块什么时候会真正降温？

美光财报之后，整个市场对存储的预期已经被彻底打满。

但我认为，现在还不是存储主线结束的时候。更准确地说，存储正在从“暴力主升浪”进入：

高位强趋势 + 产业链轮动 + 等待下一批拐点验证。

真正要关注的，不是“存储是不是周期股”这么简单，而是三个可能让市场重新定价的窗口：

SK 海力士 ADR 上市、三星 HBM4 认证、三大厂 2027–2028 扩产兑现。

⸻

1. 存储现在不是普通周期股

这轮存储强，不是传统 DRAM/NAND 涨价周期那么简单。

核心变化是：

美光、SK 海力士、三星正在从“卖 commodity memory”，变成“卖 AI 时代的战略产能”。

尤其是美光这次财报，最强的不是 Q3 beat，而是：

16 个战略客户协议；
take-or-pay；
客户预付款；
pricing floor；
管理层明确说 tight conditions 延续到 2027 年以后。

这让市场开始相信：

HBM/高端 DRAM/NAND 不再只是周期品，而是 AI 基础设施的战略资产。

但要注意：

战略资产不等于没有周期。

只是周期形态变了。

以前是：

价格一松 → EPS 暴跌 → 股价杀估值。

现在更像：

客户锁量 + 价格地板 + 多年协议 → 周期变长、变平滑，但新增供给仍然会改变议价权。

⸻

2. 第一个重要窗口：SK 海力士 ADR 上市

目前市场关注 SK 海力士可能在美国发行 ADR。

时间窗口大致在：

7 月上旬到 8 月。

有报道提到 7 月 10 日附近，也有说最快 8 月，最终还是要看 SEC / Nasdaq / 公司正式公告。

为什么这个事件重要？

因为它可能同时带来三种影响。

第一，强化存储主线。

SK 海力士是 HBM 龙头。以前很多美国资金想直接买全球 HBM 龙头并不方便，如果 ADR 上 Nasdaq，资金、ETF、期权、主动基金都会更容易交易它。

这短期可能继续推高整个 HBM 估值体系。

第二，分流美光的稀缺溢价。

过去美国投资人想买 HBM 主线，最直接就是 MU。
如果 SK 海力士可以在美股直接交易，一部分资金可能从 MU 转向 SK 海力士。

这不是基本面利空，而是板块内部资金重新分配。

第三，变成供给融资信号。

如果 SK 海力士通过 ADR 融资近 300 亿美元，并明确用于 HBM、EUV、M15X、Yongin 等产能建设，市场会开始提前交易一个问题：

2027–2028，HBM 供给会不会追上来？

所以，SK 海力士 ADR 不是“周期反转事件”，但可能是：

存储注意力峰值事件。

⸻

3. 第二个窗口：三星 HBM4 认证

三星才是真正可能改变 HBM 议价结构的变量。

原因很简单：

HBM 不是谁都能做，关键是：

$AMZN $GOOG $META $AAPL $MSFT $NVDA  The Mag 7 had a rough day, but this wasn’t a broad market panic. The selling was concentrated in the AI platform giants, with Alphabet leading the decline while Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft also came under pressure.

What’s interesting is that the market hasn’t actually favored the hyperscalers for much of this year. The bigger winners have been the companies supplying the AI buildout — semiconductor makers, networking providers, power infrastructure companies, and data center plays. In many cases, investors have been rewarding the businesses receiving AI spending rather than the ones writing the checks.

The real concern isn’t weakening AI demand. If anything, demand remains extremely strong. The concern is how much money the hyperscalers are spending to stay competitive.

Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta are pouring billions into GPUs, data centers, networking equipment, power infrastructure, and cloud capacity. Investors are starting to ask when all that spending will translate into meaningful revenue growth and stronger cash flow.

In the short term, heavy capital expenditures can pressure free cash flow. Larger infrastructure investments eventually create higher depreciation expenses, which can weigh on margins. Some companies are also issuing debt to help fund expansion, making the AI race look much more capital-intensive than the software-driven growth stories investors became accustomed to over the last decade.

The key question isn’t whether AI is real. The key question is whether these companies can generate returns on their massive AI investments that justify the spending.

Another interesting shift comes from Bank of America’s latest Global Fund Manager Survey. For years, investors viewed the Magnificent Seven as the market’s most crowded trade. That no longer appears to be the case.

A record 80% of fund managers now identify long semiconductor positions as the most crowded trade, while only 12% view the Magnificent Seven the same way. That suggests the crowding risk may have migrated from mega-cap tech into the semiconductor ecosystem.

This helps explain why semiconductor stocks have experienced such sharp pullbacks recently. When positioning becomes crowded, even small disappointments can trigger aggressive selling.

At the same time, investors continue to favor large-cap companies with high-quality earnings. That remains an important advantage for the Mag 7. These businesses still control some of the world’s strongest platforms, enjoy enormous customer bases, generate substantial cash flow, and maintain significant competitive advantages.

Perhaps the biggest change is that momentum investing is beginning to cool. Investors seem less willing to buy stocks simply because they have already gone up. Instead, they’re becoming more selective about valuation, earnings quality, and long-term fundamentals.

Valuations also look more reasonable than many headlines suggest. Excluding Tesla, several Mag 7 names such as Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft now trade much closer to broader market valuation ranges than they did during the peak AI excitement.

Could the Mag 7 fall further? Absolutely.

But for long-term investors, the more important question may be whether the market is becoming too focused on near-term AI spending while overlooking the long-term value of businesses that still dominate cloud computing, digital advertising, software, consumer technology, and increasingly, AI itself.

Sometimes the companies building the future look expensive because they’re investing heavily today. The real test is whether those investments create a larger cash-flow machine tomorrow.

post.text:
AI stock slump raises the question if investors are just taking profits or getting very nervous | Alex Veiga, AP News

Technology companies are spending big to incorporate artificial intelligence into their businesses and to build huge data centers. Investors who had jumped on the bandwagon appear to be having second thoughts.

Proponents of artificial intelligence see it as the next great revolution for the global economy. The revolution won’t come cheap. Just four companies — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Microsoft — plan to spend up to $720 billion this year, primarily on AI data centers.

This week, investors are looking at the huge sums being spent and questioning whether AI can produce the profits and productivity necessary to make all the investment worth it. Critics have been talking about the possibility of a bubble in AI investment. On Monday, Amazon and Alphabet fell about 5%.

On Tuesday, several companies that make the chips needed for the data center buildup — Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Lam Research — led the market lower.

At first, Microsoft, Alphabet and other so-called hyperscalers turned to cash on hand to fund the AI expansion. But they’re increasingly relying on the markets to raise cash.

AI buildout needs cash

Alphabet, the parent company of Google, said earlier this month that it’s raising $80 billion in cash to help pay for its investments by selling shares of its stock. Overall, Alphabet is planning to spend as much as $190 billion this year — more than all the stock of The Walt Disney Co. is worth, and Alphabet is forecasting its spending on investments next year will “significantly increase.”

In March, Amazon sold $54 billion of bonds in the U.S. and Europe as it plans to spend around $200 billion this year on AI investments.

Elon Musk’s rocket maker SpaceX was on a three-day skid heading into Tuesday. It regained some lost ground, but ended trading slightly below the closing price on its first day of trading on June 12. Musk acknowledges that SpaceX will have to spend heavily to fulfill its plans of sending AI data centers into space, and the company has announced that part of an upcoming bond offering will fund its AI buildout.

High-priced chip companies

Chip companies have benefitted as the demand for memory chips and processing power for AI data centers and other projects has led to a supply shortage and a surge in prices. Investors have bid up the share prices of these companies now in anticipation of big profits down the road. By one measure, which compares a company’s stock price to its earnings per share, these companies might look expensive.

Marvell Technologies lost money for five straight years before turning a profit of $2.7 billion in the fiscal year ended in January, thanks to gains in its data center business. The stock has more than tripled so far this year and its price-to-earnings ratio has gone from about 30 at the start of 2026 to near 100.

Some data storage companies have seen even more eye-popping gains. Sandisk shares have soared more than 700% year to date and its P/E ratio stands at 68. Whether Sandisk shares are overvalued will depend on whether it meets Wall Street’s lofty expectations for the next 12 months -- earnings per share of $188.05 per share compared with $29.16 per share for the 12 months ended March 31. When the current stock price is compared to the forecast, the price-to-earnings ratio falls to around 11.

The current price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 is around 25.

On Tuesday, investors unloaded at least some of their holdings in these stocks. Sandisk sank 13.6%, while Marvell lost 9.4%.

The sell-off also took a bite out of exchange-traded funds, or ETFs, that invest heavily in tech stocks. The Invesco QQQ Trust Series ETF was down 3.3%, while iShares Semiconductor ETF slumped 7.9%.

Pocketing some gains

While some investors may have doubts that companies going full throttle on AI infrastructure spending will ultimately be able to generate profits to justify their investment, it’s likely some of the selling this week may be investors pausing to pocket some of their gains after the stock market’s recent string of all-time highs.

“With no clear catalyst driving the move lower, we believe today’s pullback likely reflects profit-taking following a strong rally from the March lows,” said Brock Weimer, an investments strategy analyst at Edward Jones.

Big Tech gains have powered major stock indexes on record-setting runs this year. Within the S&P 500, the tech sector alone is up nearly 27% just over the last three months and roughly 17% for the year. In Asia, South Korea’s Kospi has nearly doubled so far in 2026.

Heavy selling on Tuesday triggered a halt in trading in the Kospi, which set the stage for the wave of tech stock selling when trading opened in U.S. markets, Wedbush analyst Dan Ives wrote in a research note Tuesday.

Overall AI enterprise demand in Asia is “showing no cracks in the armor, which continue to make us very bullish on owning the tech AI winners over the coming year,” he added.

Still, tech companies’ race to invest in the expansion of AI infrastructure could ultimately be sowing the seeds of future oversupply, according to Philip Straehl, chief investment officer at Morningstar Wealth.

“Periods of elevated capital investment have historically not translated into strong outcomes for investors, leaving us cautious on the outlook,” Straehl wrote in a report last week.

He expects that the rapid expansion of AI computing power will weigh on pricing, hurting companies’ returns and eventually result in a pullback in investing. Semiconductor companies are “particularly exposed to this dynamic,” Straehl wrote.

Every DRAM node shrink demands innovations in capacitor structures, cell architecture, and extremely tight process control. HBM adds another layer of complexity through TSV technology, hybrid bonding, and advanced packaging. Meanwhile, NAND continues pushing beyond 300 and even 400 stacked layers, where every additional layer raises the difficulty of deposition, etching, and yield management. GPUs are difficult to design, but producing advanced memory at scale—and continuously improving it—is often an even longer technological journey.

This perspective also explains the day’s second and third posts. According to market data, YMTC’s global NAND revenue share increased from 8% in Q1 2025 to 13% in Q1 2026, rapidly approaching the industry’s top tier. At the same time, both YMTC and CXMT are preparing IPOs and raising capital to expand manufacturing capacity while competing more aggressively on price. If these financing efforts succeed, China’s memory industry will move beyond technology catch-up into a new phase focused on gaining global market share.

Another development deserves close attention. Reports suggest YMTC has completed Apple’s supplier qualification process. If Chinese NAND products gradually enter international consumer electronics supply chains, competition within the global NAND market will intensify significantly. For years, the industry has largely been dominated by Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, and Kioxia. Continued improvements in technology and manufacturing yield from Chinese suppliers could reshape the global competitive landscape.

Later in the day, SemiVision published “AI Chips Are Hard. Memory Is Harder.” That statement effectively summarizes the entire day’s discussion.

Much of the industry’s attention remains focused on NVIDIA GPUs, AI ASICs, and advanced packaging. Yet what truly determines AI system performance is the complete memory hierarchy. From HBM4 and HBM5 to LPDDR, DDR5, SOCAMM, high-speed SSDs, and large-scale storage systems, AI requires not only more compute, but dramatically faster and larger data movement. Without sufficient memory bandwidth and capacity, even the fastest GPU spends its time waiting for data, limiting the efficiency of AI factories.

Another post shifted attention to the Korean stock market, where AI-related shares have surged as retail investors chase opportunities in AI chips and memory. SemiVision offered a more balanced perspective, asking whether this represents a sustainable long-term trend or excessive concentration of capital into a handful of semiconductor companies. AI undoubtedly creates a new investment cycle, but investors ultimately need to evaluate fundamentals—technology leadership, capital expenditures, supply-chain positioning, and profitability—rather than chasing short-term momentum.

post.text:
The memory supercycle is here — but the order is backwards from the headlines:
$MU $WDC

Everyone got hammered last week when the memory ETF dropped 12% pre-market and everything from $MU to $WDC fell 8-10%. Then Micron's earnings hit and suddenly BofA is calling this a supercycle lasting until 2027. What actually matters is who's already printing cash versus who's still riding pure narrative.

1. AI SSDs are generating actual profit right now. Enterprise SSDs for data centers hit $46 billion revenue in Q1 2026, up 90% sequentially and 246% year over year. That's more than all of 2023 combined. Server eSSD now makes up 43% of total NAND revenue and Counterpoint expects that to cross 60% by year-end. $MU and $WDC are shipping these into AI clusters today, not in 18 months. This isn't a bet on future capex — the data center buildout is already converting to revenue and gross margin expansion this quarter.

2. HBM is the tightest bottleneck but also the earliest cycle risk. High-bandwidth memory takes months to manufacture and 18-24 months to bring new cleanroom capacity online. $MU is one of the big three suppliers alongside Samsung and SK Hynix. HBM pricing is insane right now and supply can't keep up with AI accelerator demand. But here's the problem: once those fabs come online in late 2026 or 2027, you go from severe shortage to potential oversupply faster than any other memory segment. The same long lead times that create the shortage today become the reason this segment flips first when AI infrastructure spend slows.

3. Traditional DRAM and commodity NAND are riding coattails, not fundamentals. DDR4, DDR5 for PCs and phones, standard flash — these have been in a structural decline for years. The only reason pricing firmed up recently is because the big three memory makers are allocating every bit of clean capacity to HBM and eSSD. Institutions are trying to call this a "synchronized upcycle across all memory" but that's backward-looking. The moment HBM capacity comes online or hyperscalers pause orders, legacy DRAM and NAND will be the first to see price cuts and inventory builds again.

I'm long $MU for the eSSD exposure, not the HBM hype. The market is still pricing this like HBM is the entire story, but eSSD revenue is already scaling and has structurally better demand visibility through 2027 because every AI training cluster needs persistent storage, not just expensive memory. The non-consensus view: HBM peaks first and rolls over in H2 2027 when new fabs hit volume, but enterprise SSD demand keeps climbing because the data generated by all this AI compute has to live somewhere. That lag is the trade.

post.text:
Apple is raising prices across its MacBook and iPad lines. The real driver is not inflation or weak demand. It is the AI-fueled memory shortage that has been building for months.

The global supply of DRAM and NAND is tight. Hyperscalers building massive GPU clusters are taking priority access to HBM and premium memory. 

This pulls capacity away from the standard LPDDR DRAM and NAND that go into consumer devices. 

Suppliers including Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron are shifting production to higher-margin AI components. Lead times have stretched and spot prices in key segments have jumped sharply.

Apple held out longer than most. It optimized designs, managed inventory, and absorbed higher component costs. 

Tim Cook and the company have now explicitly pointed to these pressures in recent earnings calls. The unified memory architecture in M-series chips and its storage configurations make it especially exposed.

The new pricing:
- MacBook Neo: 699 dollars, up from 599
- MacBook Air: 1,299 dollars, up from 1,099
- MacBook Pro: 1,999 dollars, up from 1,699
- iPad Pro: 1,199 dollars, up from 999
- iPad Air: 749 dollars, up from 599

Apple says it is working on alternative sourcing and design changes. For now, customers are seeing the costs passed through. The MacBook Neo entry model and Mac mini were already under margin pressure. This move was almost inevitable.

The same dynamic is hitting the broader PC and tablet industry. Dell, HP, Lenovo, and others face rising component costs. Android and tablet makers will feel it too. 

Expect more adjustments through late 2026, either through outright increases or quieter moves like fewer base configurations and higher storage tiers.

This is the pattern you have tracked closely. AI demand is succeeding so much that it is constraining the rest of the ecosystem. 

The "AI tax" is now reaching everyday devices after years of server-first allocation.

It will be interesting to watch how quickly consumer memory pricing stabilizes once HBM supply ramps. 

Do you think these hikes will stick, or will design optimizations and new capacity bring relief sooner than expected?
